To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the brain areas that are involved in the maintenance of VSTM are different for different ways of presenting the to-be-memorized items, and that these differences are related to the way the brain processes the information in these areas.
sequencing and repeating visual stimuli increase VSTM capacity by reducing competition between objects in the display.

sequencing and repeating visual displays overcomes bottlenecks of attentional control during simultaneous encoding by reducing competition between nonattended objects and allowing reallocation of attentional resources.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how attention and memory interact.
the neural correlates of the capacity limits of VSTM, with a focus on the mechanisms underlying the capacity gain for sequenced and repeated displays.
the question of how visual information is selected for further processing.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
VSTM gain is due to a reduction of interference from nonattended items in a display, and that this is achieved by either top-down attentional reallocation or stimulus-driven attentional capture.
the results of this study provide evidence for a role of attention in VSTM.
our results show that the visual system has a limited capacity to process visual information, which can be overcome by the use of attentional strategies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the neural mechanisms underlying the improvement in VSTM for repeated and sequenced displays are distinct and that these improvements are mediated by different neural mechanisms.

visual short term memory is limited by the attentional resources allocated to the objects in the visual scene, and that the brain can compensate for these limitations by increasing the attentional control over the objects.
visual attentional control and stimulus-driven processes interact to determine VSTM capacity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
attentional control is a crucial component for understanding the mechanisms underlying visual short-term memory.
VSTM gain for repeated and sequenced displays is due to a combination of stimulus-driven and controlled processes.
the brain is not a single processor but a set of multiple processors that are able to work in parallel, and that the brain can dynamically adjust the allocation of resources to different processors.
